title: Input Capture: Credential API Hooking
summary: Credential API hooking intercepts the programming interfaces that handle authentication so that the parameters carrying usernames, passwords or tokens are copied as they pass through. On Windows the interception can be implemented with hook procedures that receive events such as messages and keystrokes, with import address table patching that changes the stored pointers a process uses for its imported functions, or with inline hooks that overwrite the first bytes of a function so execution jumps elsewhere. On Linux and macOS the same outcome is often reached by forcing a shared library into a program's address space through the preload or insert libraries environment settings, then replacing a library function that authentication code calls, such as the read function used by remote shell and copy tools. The result is targeted rather than indiscriminate, because only calls carrying secrets are touched. Detection is memory focused and looks for modified function prologues, import tables or module lists pointing outside known libraries, unexpected preloaded libraries on a process, and credential handling processes loading code absent from their shipped installation.

beginner.definition: Credential API hooking means quietly changing the way a program asks the system to check a password. A programming interface, or API, is the set of commands one program uses to ask another program for help. The attacker replaces part of that conversation so the password is copied while it travels through. The program still works normally afterwards, so the user never notices anything.
beginner.whyItMatters: This method is more selective than recording every key press, because it only touches the calls that carry credentials. It can run inside trusted programs such as mail clients and remote access tools. The program keeps working, so nothing appears broken and users never complain to support. Finding it requires memory inspection rather than ordinary file scanning. You should know about it because it defeats the idea that only the filesystem matters.
howItWorks: Programs use programming interfaces, called APIs, to ask the system to check credentials.
The attacker replaces a small part of that interface so the call passes through their code.
One method rewrites the table that stores the addresses of imported functions.
Another overwrites the first bytes of the function itself, which is called inline hooking.
On Linux and macOS, an environment variable can force an extra library into the program.
The copied credentials are saved, and the original function may still run so nothing breaks.
beginner.example: Imagine a post office where every parcel is weighed at one counter before it travels onward. A worker quietly replaces the scale with a lookalike scale. Parcels still get weighed, labels still print, and deliveries still arrive on time. The only difference is that the lookalike writes down the weight and address of everything passing across it. The queue moves exactly as before, so no customer or manager has any reason to suspect the counter.
takeaways: Hooking targets the exact functions that carry credentials rather than all typing.
It can be done by changing function pointers, function code or loaded libraries.
Detection usually needs memory and module inspection, not only file scanning.

objectives: Explain what an API is and why credential handling functions are worth hooking.
Describe import address table hooking and inline hooking in plain terms.
Explain how a preloaded shared library achieves the same result on other systems.
Identify memory artefacts that reveal a hooked credential function.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from ordinary keylogging.
